title: Fractional Exponents
short: x^(1/n) means the nth root of x, and x^(m/n) its mth power.

blocks.html: You know the exponent rules for whole-number exponents, and you know cube roots. What could an exponent like $\frac{1}{2}$ or $\frac{2}{3}$ mean? We get to choose, and the wise choice is the one that keeps the old rules working.

The power-of-a-power rule says $(x^a)^b = x^{ab}$. If that is to hold for $a = \frac{1}{2}$, then $\left(x^{1/2}\right)^2 = x^{1} = x$. So $x^{1/2}$ must be a number whose square is $x$: that is $\sqrt{x}$. In the same way, $\left(x^{1/3}\right)^3 = x$, so $x^{1/3} = \sqrt[3]{x}$. And $x^{2/3} = \left(x^{1/3}\right)^2$: take the cube root, then square. Every other meaning would break a rule we already trust.

head: Exponent
$8^{\text{exponent}}$
How
blocks.cap: Each step of $\frac{1}{3}$ in the exponent multiplies by $\sqrt[3]{8} = 2$, just as whole-number steps multiply by $8$.

blocks.html: $x^{1/n} = \sqrt[n]{x}$ and $x^{m/n} = \left(\sqrt[n]{x}\right)^m = \sqrt[n]{x^m}$. The denominator is the root, the numerator is the power. A negative exponent still means a reciprocal.

blocks.title: A negative exponent
steps: The negative exponent means the reciprocal: $27^{-2/3} = \frac{1}{9}$.

blocks.title: Change forms
steps: The root index $5$ goes in the denominator, the power $3$ in the numerator.

blocks.html: Computing $8^{1/3}$ as $\frac{8}{3}$, or $16^{3/4}$ as $16 \cdot \frac{3}{4} = 12$. An exponent is never multiplied into the base. Check by undoing: if $8^{1/3}$ were $\frac{8}{3}$, then cubing it would give back $8$, but $\left(\frac{8}{3}\right)^3 \approx 19$.
